extracted.intended_audience: inventors, small companies, and clients seeking to obtain UK patent protection
extracted.subtask_description: A practitioner-oriented overview of the procedural steps, substantive patentability requirements, timing deadlines, fees, and options (national/EP/PCT) for obtaining and maintaining a UK patent. Intended to guide applicants and advise on attorney services, searches, and post-filing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent definition, territoriality and term
rubrics_metrics.description: A Patent is a legal monopoly giving an inventor (or his employer) the right to prevent others making, selling, importing or otherwise using his invention for a maximum of 20 years. Patents are territorial and the present document relates only to the UK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the basic expectation that patent rights are limited by time (up to 20 years) and apply country-by-country; applicants must consider UK-specific procedures and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable in the UK ... an invention must be new at the date of filing the first patent application describing the invention. This means that the invention must not have been made available to the public by the inventor or any other party before the date of application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is essential to consider whether a UK patent application should be filed before going to market or otherwise publicising the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must also be sufficiently different to what is already known so as to be more than an obvious development – it must have an 'inventive step'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment against prior art focuses not only on novelty but whether the invention would have been an obvious development to a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical subject-matter / excluded subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent protection is only applicable to technical matters. Some ideas or inventions do not qualify. These include the mere discovery of a new use or property, a written or artistic or musical work (they fall under copyright), rules of playing a game, a scheme of doing business, a manner of presenting information, or a computer program (but many computer programs are protected through patents, so please seek full advice if an invention involves a computer program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should evaluate whether their invention is a technical solution; borderline cases (e.g., computer programs, business methods) require specialist advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of patent attorneys / scope of attorney services
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, we prepare the description and claims for you (called a specification) and after obtaining your approval and making any adjustments we attend to all the paperwork for submitting an application to the UK Patent Office. We keep a detailed diary for your application and seek your instructions in good time before various deadlines and significant-cost-incurring matters arise. We deal with all the formalities and correspondence with the UK Patent Office, keep you informed and seek your comments as required at each stage. We can also advise on many related matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent attorneys handle drafting, filing, prosecution, diary management and correspondence; they charge professional time (usually hourly) and may offer additional advisory services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and billing components
rubrics_metrics.description: Our bills comprise three components: (a) a charge based on our professional time spent on the matter; (b) a service charge, being a flat rate administrative charge specific to the particular job done and covering mainly clerical matters; and (c) disbursements (e.g. UKIPO fees, draughtsman’s charges, foreign attorneys’ charges, telephone, copying, fax and travel costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional time is recorded and most charges can only be estimated; some fees (e.g., service charges, specific office fees) may be fixed amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum filing content and UK filing date / priority year
rubrics_metrics.description: The first stage is to file a patent application at the UK Intellectual Property Office ... consisting of at least a description of the invention and drawings (if appropriate). Filing a patent application in the UK generates a 'UK filing date' from which runs a 'priority year'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UK filing date triggers timing deadlines (priority year) for foreign filings and other actions; ensure the description and drawings adequately disclose the invention at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search fee and claims filing deadline (within priority year)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the priority year, the UKIPO makes no examination of the application until a search fee is paid and patent claims are filed. This is usually done at the time of filing the application but must be done on or before the first anniversary of the UK filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must pay the search fee and file claims by the first anniversary to preserve examination rights; plan filing strategy accordingly if delaying claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second application for improvements claiming priority
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are any improvements or modifications to the invention during the priority year, these may be included in a second UK patent application. The second application claims priority from the first application and is entitled to the UK filing date of the first application for subject matter which is common to both applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subsequent applications to capture developments, but only common subject matter benefits from the earlier filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search procedure and search report
rubrics_metrics.description: After the search fee has been paid, an Examiner at the UKIPO conducts a search through previously published patent specifications and a limited range of other literature to identify published documents which may be relevant to the novelty or obviousness of the invention. A search report listing these documents is sent to the applicant about four months after the search fee has been paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The search report is used to assess the prospect of the patent application being granted; applicants should review report and consider next steps (examination, withdrawal, amendments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and possibility to prevent publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately eighteen months after the first UK filing date, the patent application is published together with the search report. If the search report was favourable and the prospect of securing a granted patent seems good, the applicant may decide to proceed to the detailed examination stage. If the search report was unfavourable and the application is withdrawn within about 15 months of the first UK filing date, publication can be prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can avoid publication by timely withdrawal (around 15 months) if prospects are poor; publication is otherwise automatic at ~18 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination fee timing and Examination Report
rubrics_metrics.description: Within six months of the date of publication of the application, an examination fee must be paid. The application is then allocated to a UKIPO Examiner who will issue an Examination Report detailing any objections to the application. Objections which may arise are that the invention is not new or is merely an obvious departure from what is already known. There may also be editorial objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay the examination fee promptly after publication to enter substantive examination; expect objections on novelty, inventive step, or form and prepare to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to objections and prosecution timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant has a time limit (usually six months) to file a response to the objections by argument that the objections are wrong or misplaced, or by amending the application to overcome the objections. There may be several exchanges of correspondence and this procedure is referred to as 'prosecution of the application'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for multiple rounds of amendment/argument; observe response deadlines (typically six months) to avoid adverse consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to combine search and examination (expedited route)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to combine the search and examination stages by paying the search and examination fees at the same time. This variation of normal procedure may be useful if the applicant requires a patent to be granted earlier than would otherwise be the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combined payment to accelerate grant when faster prosecution is required, recognizing additional immediate fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: On successful completion of the examination stage, the UK patent application is formally accepted and the application in its accepted form is published as a granted UK patent. Typically this takes place some three to four years after the UK filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multi-year timescale from filing to grant (commonly 3–4 years); plan commercial strategy around this timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal (maintenance) fees
rubrics_metrics.description: On the fourth and each subsequent anniversary of its UK filing date, renewal fees are payable to keep the granted UK patent in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for ongoing renewal fees from year four onwards to maintain enforceable rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for foreign protection and priority treatment (national / EP / PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If patents are required to protect export markets or manufacturing interests abroad, there are three options available to obtain foreign protection: (a) filing foreign national patent applications in each foreign country where protection is required, (b) filing a European patent application designating one or more European countries where protection is required, and (c) filing an International patent application under the Patent Co-operation Treaty (a 'PCT application') designating one or more countries or regions worldwide where protection is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application filed on or before the first anniversary of the UK filing date by any of these options is treated as having effectively been filed on the UK filing date (priority). Seek advice on cost/procedure differences among options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-filing novelty searches (character and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: We can also arrange pre-filing novelty searches through patent literature to assess whether an invention is new. Such a novelty search is wide-ranging, but is not targeted precisely – it uses a shot-gun approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty searches are useful before major investment or multiple foreign filings; they likely find patents representing obvious infringement risks but cannot guarantee that all relevant patents have been identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement clearance search (targeted search when certainty required)
rubrics_metrics.description: If more certainty is required that taking certain specified commercial steps will not infringe a patent already existing, then an infringement clearance search is required. We can arrange this kind of search also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use infringement clearance searches to obtain higher confidence on freedom-to-operate for specific commercial activities; these are more precise and targeted than broad novelty searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation risk and insurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of patent litigation in the UK is high. Whilst the vast majority of UK patents are never involved in litigation, the inventor or small company with limited funds may wish to insure against the costs of patent litigation. Insurance is available to assist with the legal costs of instigating a patent action or of defending a patent action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider litigation insurance especially if resources are limited; request further details from advisors as needed.
